text_blocks.snippet: Both ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) and ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers) are recognized as major first-line drug classes for managing high blood pressure (hypertension), alongside calcium channel blockers and thiazide diuretics .
snippet_highlighted_words: Both ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors) and ARBs (angiotensin II receptor blockers) are recognized as major first-line drug classes for managing high blood pressure (hypertension)

list.snippet: Blood Pressure Efficacy: Both classes lower blood pressure and reduce systemic vascular resistance to a similar extent by targeting the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
Cardiovascular & Renal Protection: Both offer significant benefits in protecting the heart and kidneys, especially in patients with diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or heart failure.
Combinations: They must never be taken together in combination due to a higher risk of hyperkalemia and kidney injury.

text_blocks.snippet: Key Differences & Why ARBs Are Often Preferred First-Line

list.snippet: ACE inhibitors block the enzyme that converts angiotensin I into angiotensin II .
ARBs block angiotensin II directly from binding to its receptor sites (AT₁).

ACE inhibitors (ending in -pril, such as lisinopril) commonly cause a persistent, dry, nagging cough (affecting up to 10%–20% of patients) due to a buildup of bradykinin, and carry a risk of angioedema (swelling of the lips, face, or throat).
ARBs (ending in -sartan, such as losartan) do not affect bradykinin breakdown, meaning they have a significantly lower rate of dry cough and a much lower risk of angioedema .

Guideline & Clinical Shift: While traditional guidelines (such as ACC/AHA and ESC/ESH) historically placed ACE inhibitors and ARBs on equal footing, large comparative studies (published via JAMA Network and Annals of Internal Medicine ) show identical cardiovascular efficacy with a much more favorable side effect and adherence profile for ARBs. As a result, many clinicians now preferentially start with an ARB.

references.title: Antihypertensive Treatment and Development of Heart Failure in Hypertension
references.snippet: To our knowledge, our study is the largest network meta-analysis ever performed in essential hypertension, and it was aimed specifically at investigating the efficacy of different antihypertensive strategies in the prevention of HF. The main finding of our analysis is that all antihypertensive strategies are better than placebo in HF prevention, with the exception of α-blockers. Diuretics and RAS inhibitors (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) are the most effective class of drugs, a diuretic-based treatment being the more effective first-line antihypertensive intervention for preventing HF. Our analysis also shows that CCBs and β-blockers are significantly less effective than diuretics as first-line agents, and they tend to be inferior to RAS inhibitors. These results do not seem to be significantly influenced by age and sex, as highlighted by our subanalyses (Table 4).

references.title: The Difficult Task of Finding the Best Antihypertensive Agent
references.snippet: In this issue of the Archives, Sciarretta et al present the results from a Bayesian network meta-analysis with respect to possible differences of individual antihypertensive strategies regarding the prevention of HF. They report on 223 313 individuals included in 26 antihypertensive trials. Of these, 186 378 individuals (83.5%) had an established diagnosis of arterial hypertension on inclusion in the respective trials, and a total of 8554 individuals (3.8%) were diagnosed as having HF during the course of their respective study. The main result is that diuretics and ACE inhibitors/ARBs were the most effective treatment and should therefore be considered first-line therapy with respect to HF prevention.
